user_message:
A university's commercial team has identified a highly specialised piece of research equipment and support services that, in their assessment, only one particular provider can currently deliver. They intend to award the contract directly rather than run a competition, given the unique technical situation, but want to know what must be published before signing anything, so that the decision is transparent and can be scrutinised by anyone who disagrees with it.

We think only one supplier can realistically deliver this specialist research contract, so we're planning to award it directly without competition. What do we need to publish before we actually sign the contract with them?

A council submitted a standard contract notice for an open procedure works contract for publication in January 2025, before the main procurement law reform commenced on 24 February 2025. The competition is still running and the council now expects to reach contract award only in late 2026. The procurement officer needs to know which set of procurement rules - the ones in force when the notice was submitted, or the ones now in force - govern the rest of the process, including award and standstill.

We published our tender notice for this contract back in January 2025, before the procurement rules changed, but we're only going to finish the competition and award the contract now. Which set of rules do we need to follow to finish this off - the ones that were in force when we started, or the current ones?

A council has run a competitive tendering procedure for a highways maintenance contract and has identified its preferred bidder. Before proceeding further, the commercial team needs to establish exactly what must be published to the market to record the intention to enter into the contract, and whether unsuccessful bidders whose tenders were assessed are entitled to receive any individual feedback before that notice is published.

We've picked our preferred bidder for a highways contract after running a full competitive tender. What do we need to publish to record that decision, and do we owe the unsuccessful bidders any kind of individual feedback before we publish it?

A main contractor delivering a council-funded regeneration scheme has been taking more than 60 days to pay its specialist subcontractors, several of whom have complained to the council's contract management team about cash-flow strain.

Our main contractor is dragging its heels paying its subcontractors on this scheme - do the prompt payment rules we imposed on the main contract actually reach down to protect the subcontractors too, and do the subcontractors have any separate right to charge interest on the late amounts?

A central government department drafting award criteria for a facilities services contract wants to give significant scoring weight to whether bidders commit to paying all staff assigned to the contract the real living wage, as part of the department's social value ambitions.

Can we build a meaningful chunk of the scoring around whether bidders will commit to paying the real living wage to the staff working on this contract, or would that be going beyond what we're allowed to assess tenders on?

A council is about to issue a six-million-pound call-off contract for highways resurfacing works under an existing regional framework that several other authorities also use. The framework agreement itself already sets high-level performance standards for participating contractors.

Given the framework we're calling off from already has its own performance regime built in, do we still need to separately set our own key performance indicators on this individual piece of work, or does the framework-level arrangement already cover that requirement for us?

We're evaluating tenders for a school catering contract using a mix of price and quality scores. Before we commit to a supplier we want to make sure our approach to picking the winner, and telling people about the decision, is legally sound.

When comparing tenders on things like price and quality, is there a legal requirement about how we go about deciding who wins, and do we have to tell people publicly who we've picked before the contract is actually signed?

A journalist has submitted a request asking for the full pricing schedule from a contract we recently awarded. The winning supplier has written to us saying the figures are commercially sensitive and should not be released. We need to decide how to respond to the request.

Someone outside the organisation has asked to see detailed pricing from one of our live supplier contracts, and the supplier objects to it being released. What are the grounds, if any, for keeping that information back, and what would we need to be able to show to rely on them rather than just asserting it?

We are running a competition and have learned that one of our shortlisted bidders is currently the subject of a central government inquiry that could eventually see it shut out of public contracts everywhere. No final decision has been made yet, and the bidder is not on any published list. We need to work out whether we must wait for that central process to finish before we can make our own call on this bidder within our competition.

One of our bidders is currently the subject of a central inquiry that could eventually see them barred from all public contracts, but that hasn't been decided yet and they're not on any published list. Do we have to wait for that process to finish before we can make our own call on this bidder, or can we act now within our own competition?

A department is running a competitive flexible procedure for a complex digital transformation contract using two tendering rounds. First-round submissions were disappointing, and a well-regarded specialist supplier who missed the first-round deadline has since asked to be let into round two. Separately, the team has learned that one of the remaining bidders plans to sub-contract part of the work to a firm connected to a supplier exclusion issue.

Can we bring a new supplier into the later round of our procedure given how weak the field was, and separately, what do we need to do before we can exclude a bidder over a problem linked to its proposed sub-contractor?

An NHS trust has had a critical piece of imaging equipment fail without warning, creating an immediate patient-safety risk. Clinical leads say a replacement must be sourced and installed within days, which rules out running any kind of competition at all.

Given how urgent and unavoidable this is, can we award a contract directly without competing it, and does the usual wait before we're allowed to sign the contract still apply in a case like this?

A department published a contract change notice to modify an existing IT services contract on agreed grounds, and gave the standard standstill period before making the change. Partway through that standstill period, a disappointed third party notified the department that it has issued court proceedings challenging the planned modification.

Now that a challenge has formally been issued and we've been notified of it during this waiting period, are we still free to go ahead with the change, and how does that interact with the standstill period we already gave?

A registered social housing provider awarded a six-year IT managed services contract in 2023 through a competitive procedure run under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015; the contract runs until 2029. The Procurement Act 2023 has since commenced. The IT supplier has just been acquired by a new corporate parent, and the provider's legal team is concerned that, under today's exclusion rules, the new ownership structure would be treated as a red flag if the same supplier were bidding for a contract now.

We awarded this contract a couple of years before the new Procurement Act rules came in, and it doesn't expire for a while yet. The company delivering it has just changed ownership, and the new structure looks like something that would count against them if they were bidding today. Does that ownership change give us a right to terminate the contract now, or are we limited to whatever termination grounds applied under the rules that were in force when we ran the original competition?

A regional water and sewerage utility company ran a competitive tendering procedure for a specialist leak-detection technology contract. Of the two tenders received, neither met the minimum technical pass mark set out in the tender documents, so both were disregarded in the evaluation. The utility still needs the service and does not want to abandon the requirement.

We ran a competitive tender for a specialist technical service, and neither of the two bids we got met our minimum quality bar, so neither could be taken forward. We still need this work done and don't want to just walk away from the requirement. Can we move to negotiating and awarding the contract directly to one of the bidders instead of starting the whole competition again, and if so, what do we need to do first?

A central government department has a below-threshold consultancy contract, awarded under the Procurement Act 2023 regime, worth about £45,000. It is not a concession, framework or utilities contract. Partway through delivery, the department wants to extend the contract term by six months and add a modest amount of extra scope; the change would not push the contract's value up to the level of a public contract. The department's policy team has been told that any change to a contract must be justified against one of the Act's formal permitted modification grounds, in the same way as for its largest contracts.

We have a below-threshold consultancy contract that we'd like to extend by six months and add a bit of extra scope, and the change would still leave it comfortably under the value where it would count as a full public contract. Do we need to justify this change against one of the Act's formal modification grounds, the same way we would for one of our larger contracts, or is there more flexibility for a contract of this size?

A water utility runs a framework for recurring minor capital works and, rather than closing it after a single round of tenders, wants a structure that lets it reopen the competition to new entrants periodically over several years without re-running the whole procurement from scratch each time. The commercial team wants to understand the practical rules for how often it must reopen the arrangement, how long each round can last, and what happens to suppliers already appointed when it does.

We run a framework for recurring minor works and want a structure that lets us periodically reopen it to new suppliers over several years instead of closing it after one round. What are the practical rules for how often we have to reopen it, how long each round can last, and what happens to the suppliers already on it when we do?

A central government department ran a full open competitive tender for a bespoke case-management IT system, but every bid received was either non-compliant with the mandatory technical requirements or showed signs of coordinated pricing between two bidders. The department is now under pressure to have a working system in place within a tight statutory deadline and is asking whether it can move straight to negotiating with one of the disqualified suppliers, or must start the whole tender again.

We ran a full competitive tender for a bespoke system, but none of the bids we received were usable -- some failed our mandatory requirements and we also have concerns about coordinated pricing between two bidders. We're under real time pressure. Can we move to a direct award without starting a fresh competition, and if so, what do we need to check and publish before we do?

A council is roughly a year into a three-year highways resurfacing and drainage contract when a routine survey uncovers unexpected soil contamination beneath one section of road, requiring substantially more remediation work than the original scope covered. The contract does not include any provision anticipating this kind of ground condition, and the contract manager needs the existing contractor to start the additional remediation quickly rather than losing months to a fresh procurement.

Partway through our highways contract, a survey has revealed contamination requiring significantly more remedial work than we originally scoped, and the contract didn't anticipate this. Can we instruct our existing contractor to do the extra work without running a new procurement, and is there a limit on how much extra value we can add this way?

A contract manager at an NHS body has just published the contract award notice for a large clinical support services contract. An unsuccessful bidder has emailed asking pointed questions about the evaluation, and a colleague has suggested going ahead and signing the contract straight away since the unsuccessful bidders have already been told the outcome informally. The contract manager wants to check whether there is actually a required waiting period before the contract can be signed.

We've just published our contract award notice - is there a legally required waiting period before we're allowed to actually sign the contract, or can we go ahead now that bidders have been told the outcome? If there is a wait, how long is it and what's the actual legal basis, not just what my colleague assumes?

A central government department awarded a five-year IT managed services contract in 2022, well before the most recent overhaul of the procurement rules, following a standard competitive tendering procedure. The contract is still live. Rising subcontractor costs mean the department is now considering a price increase of roughly 12% together with the addition of a new, previously unspecified support tier, and would prefer to do this without launching a fresh procurement. The contract manager assumes that because the wider procurement rules have since changed, the new rules must now govern any changes to the contract.

We're looking at increasing the price on one of our contracts by around 12% and adding a new support tier, and we'd rather not run a whole new procurement for that. The contract was awarded a while back, before the procurement rules changed -- does that affect which modification rules apply, and would a change like this be allowed without a new competition?
